rock-pigeon.young: Both parents raise one or two squabs, feeding them "crop milk" they make in their own throats. The squabs leave the nest at about a month old, already pigeon-sized.
rock-pigeon.social: Couples usually stay together for life and do everything as a pair. They live in easygoing flocks where sharing a sidewalk snack is normal.

spring.title: A nest on the ledge
spring.body: Pigeon couples are raising squabs on ledges and under bridges. Dad usually sits on the eggs by day, Mom takes the night shift.

summer.title: Brood after brood
summer.body: City pigeons can raise babies all year. Last month's squabs are already out walking the sidewalk with the flock.

fall.title: Teens in the flock
fall.body: Young pigeons have blended into the flock. You can tell them by their duller necks and the way they still flutter at their parents now and then.

winter.title: Cozy couples
winter.body: Pairs stay side by side through the cold, puffed up on sunny ledges. Some even start a winter nest.

house-sparrow.young: Both parents feed the chicks bugs (seeds are too tough for babies). Chicks leave the nest after about two weeks and beg from the hedge for a while longer.
house-sparrow.social: Very social: they nest close together in loose colonies and chatter in the same hedge all day. Many pairs stay together year after year.

spring.title: House hunting
spring.body: Couples are claiming nooks in walls, signs and vents and stuffing them with grass, feathers and the odd bit of string.

summer.title: Bug delivery
summer.body: Parents are running nonstop bug deliveries to fluffy fledglings who sit in the hedge flapping and yelling. Many raise two or three broods.

fall.title: The gang
fall.body: This year's young have joined big chattering flocks. Family ties loosen, but nobody's ever alone in a sparrow hedge.

winter.title: Group huddle
winter.body: Flocks roost together in thick ivy and evergreens, puffed up for warmth. Couples often stick together through the winter.

eastern-gray-squirrel.young: Mom raises the babies alone in a leafy nest or a tree hole. They open their eyes at about a month and are out on their own around three months old.
eastern-gray-squirrel.social: Mostly solo, but easygoing about sharing a tree. On cold nights a few may even pile into one nest together.

spring.title: Babies in the nest
spring.body: Late-winter babies are peeking out of their leafy nests. Mom does all the work; Dad isn't part of the picture.

summer.title: A second litter
summer.body: Many moms have a second litter now, while spring's kids practice leaping and burying things not quite right.

fall.title: Out on their own
fall.body: This year's young are on their own, burying acorns like pros and looking for a spot to call home.

winter.title: Chase season
winter.body: Midwinter is courting time: you'll see dizzy chases spiraling up the trunks. Some squirrels share a nest to stay warm.

european-starling.young: Both parents feed the chicks in a hole or a cranny. Fledglings follow their parents around the lawn, begging loudly with their beaks wide open.
european-starling.social: About as social as birds get: they feed in crowds, sleep in crowds and fly in the swirling crowds called murmurations.

spring.title: Decorating the nest
spring.body: Starling couples are nesting in holes and crannies. The males tuck in fresh green leaves and petals, which may help keep bugs away.

summer.title: Brown teenagers
summer.body: This year's young are plain brown and travel in noisy gangs of their own, probing lawns together.

fall.title: The big swirl
fall.body: Families melt into huge flocks. At dusk they swirl over the marshes in murmurations before settling in to sleep.

winter.title: Thousands to a roost
winter.body: They sleep packed together by the thousands under bridges and in thick trees, then head out in groups at sunrise.

mourning-dove.young: Both parents raise two squabs on crop milk in a famously flimsy nest. The babies leave at about two weeks, and the parents may start the next pair right away.
mourning-dove.social: Couples stay close and preen each other. In winter they gather in quiet flocks on wires and feeders.

spring.title: A wobbly nest
spring.body: Couples are building nests so thin you can see the eggs through them. It works anyway: both parents take turns sitting.

summer.title: Round after round
summer.body: Doves can raise five or more broods a year here. The parents barely pause between pairs of squabs.

fall.title: Young on the wire
fall.body: This year's young sit in rows on the wires with the grown-ups. You can tell them by the pale edges on their feathers.

winter.title: Quiet flocks
winter.body: Doves gather in calm little flocks, fluffed up side by side on a sunny branch.

american-robin.young: Mom builds a mud-lined cup and sits on the eggs; both parents feed the chicks worms. When the chicks leave, Dad often takes them under his wing while Mom starts the next nest.
american-robin.social: Territorial singers in spring, but in fall and winter they join flocks that roam for berries together.

spring.title: Blue eggs
spring.body: Robins are building mud cups in trees and on ledges. Inside: three or four eggs in the famous robin's-egg blue.

summer.title: Dad's in charge
summer.body: Spotty-breasted fledglings hop after their dad on the lawn while Mom works on the next nest.

fall.title: Berry flocks
fall.body: Robins drop their territories and team up in flocks, moving from tree to tree to eat the berries.

winter.title: Winter crew
winter.body: Many robins stay all winter in roaming flocks. They're quieter now, eating fruit in the treetops instead of worms.

herring-gull.young: Both parents raise two or three chicks, often on rooftops here. A chick taps the red spot on a parent's bill to ask for food. Young gulls stay brown for years.
herring-gull.social: They nest in colonies and many couples reunite every spring. Out of breeding season they loaf in big mixed groups.

spring.title: Rooftop colonies
spring.body: Gull couples are reuniting and claiming nesting spots on islands and flat roofs.

summer.title: Fuzzy chicks
summer.body: Speckled chicks are tapping the red spot on their parents' bills: the gull way of saying "feed me, please."

fall.title: Brown kids
fall.body: The young are flying now, all brown and mottled. It takes them about four years to grow into the gray-and-white grown-up look.

winter.title: Big hangouts
winter.body: Gulls of every age gather in big, noisy groups on the piers and parking lots.

raccoon.young: Mom raises the kits alone in a hollow tree, chimney or attic. They follow her out at night by early summer and usually stay with her through their first winter.
raccoon.social: Mostly solo grown-ups, but moms and kits are a tight team, and neighbors' ranges overlap without much fuss.

spring.title: Kits in the den
spring.body: Raccoon kits are being born in hollow trees and the odd attic. Mom stays close; Dad isn't involved.

summer.title: Night school
summer.body: Moms lead their kits out at night, often in single file, teaching them what's good to eat and where to climb.

fall.title: Almost grown
fall.body: The kits are nearly as big as Mom now, but many still tag along with her on her rounds.

winter.title: Family den
winter.body: On the coldest nights, a mom and her grown kits often curl up together in one den. The kits head off on their own in spring.

monarch.young: No babysitting: Mom lays her eggs one at a time on milkweed and flies on. Each caterpillar is on its own from the moment it hatches.
monarch.social: Solo most of the year, but on migration they gather by the dozens or hundreds to sleep in the same trees.

spring.title: First eggs
spring.body: The first monarchs arrive from the south and lay eggs, one per milkweed leaf. The caterpillars never meet their mom.

summer.title: Generation after generation
summer.body: Several short-lived generations are born here, each laying eggs for the next.

fall.title: The great trip south
fall.body: This fall's monarchs are a special generation that flies all the way to Mexico. They stop to sleep in clusters along the way.

winter.title: Together in the mountains
winter.body: Millions spend the winter packed together on fir trees in Mexico's mountains, waiting for spring.

red-tailed-hawk.young: Both parents raise two or three chicks in a big stick nest high on a tree or building. After the young fly, they stay near their parents for weeks learning to hunt.
red-tailed-hawk.social: Couples often stay together for years and share a territory all year. Mostly they keep to themselves.

spring.title: High-rise nest
spring.body: Hawk couples are fixing up big stick nests on ledges and tall trees. One parent is almost always sitting.

summer.title: Flying lessons
summer.body: The young are out of the nest, loud and clumsy, following their parents and begging for food.

fall.title: On their own
fall.body: This year's young head off to find their own place. You can tell them by their brown, banded tails: no red until next year.

winter.title: Couple's territory
winter.body: Pairs stay on their home turf all winter, perched together on the same tall spots.

blue-jay.young: Both parents raise the chicks, and the family keeps traveling together for weeks after they leave the nest.
blue-jay.social: Loud, chatty families. Some couples stay together for life, and jays team up to mob hawks and owls.

spring.title: Quiet nesting
spring.body: Usually noisy jays go strangely quiet near their nests, so no one finds them.

summer.title: Family outings
summer.body: Families travel together through the trees, the young still begging from their parents.

fall.title: Flocks on the move
fall.body: Some jays fly south in loose flocks along the coast; others stay. Everyone's burying acorns.

winter.title: The neighborhood watch
winter.body: Jays stay in small groups and shout a warning together when a hawk shows up.

dark-eyed-junco.young: Juncos raise their chicks in nests on the ground in northern forests and mountains, far from here. We only meet them in winter.
dark-eyed-junco.social: In winter they live in flocks with a pecking order: everyone knows who gets the best seeds first.

spring.title: Heading north
spring.body: The flocks break up and the juncos fly north to nest. The males start singing before they leave.

summer.title: Far away
summer.body: Our juncos are raising chicks in nests tucked on the ground in northern forests.

fall.title: Back with friends
fall.body: They arrive in flocks, flashing their white tail feathers as they hop under the hedges.

winter.title: Pecking order
winter.body: Each flock has a pecking order. The top juncos get the best spots under the feeder; the rest wait their turn.

virginia-opossum.young: Babies the size of a honeybee crawl into Mom's pouch. After about two months they ride on her back, then go off on their own at three or four months.
virginia-opossum.social: Solo wanderers. They don't keep territories and mostly just mind their own business.

spring.title: Pouch babies
spring.body: Moms are carrying tiny babies in their pouches. Some have more than a dozen in there.

summer.title: Piggyback rides
summer.body: Bigger babies ride on Mom's back, holding on to her fur as she shuffles along.

fall.title: Off they go
fall.body: The young are on their own now, each wandering off to find a place to live.

winter.title: Solo and snug
winter.body: Opossums sleep alone in a cozy den on the coldest days, coming out on milder nights.

american-crow.young: Both parents raise the chicks, and often last year's kids stay home to help: bringing food and standing guard for their new brothers and sisters.
american-crow.social: Crows live in close family groups and know each other well. In winter, families join huge evening roosts with thousands of other crows.

spring.title: Big siblings help
spring.body: Crow families are building nests, and older siblings often pitch in with the twigs and the snacks.

summer.title: Blue-eyed kids
summer.body: Fledglings follow their family around, begging loudly. Young crows have blue-gray eyes that turn dark later.

fall.title: The evening commute
fall.body: At dusk, families fly together toward big group roosts, calling the whole way.

winter.title: Thousands together
winter.body: Crows sleep in roosts of thousands, but each family still sticks close together inside the crowd.

white-throated-sparrow.young: They nest on the ground up north in Canada's forests. Here, we only see them in fall, winter and spring.
white-throated-sparrow.social: Winter flocks. They come in white-striped and tan-striped versions, and pairs are almost always one of each.

spring.title: Singing to leave
spring.body: They practice their "Oh sweet Canada" song before flying north to nest.

summer.title: Up north
summer.body: They're raising chicks on the ground in northern forests, far from the city.

fall.title: Back in flocks
fall.body: Flocks arrive and settle under hedges and in park edges, scratching through the leaves together.

winter.title: One of each
winter.body: Winter flocks mix white-striped and tan-striped birds. When they pair up in spring, it's almost always one of each.

chimney-swift.young: Both parents raise the chicks in a little nest glued to the inside of a chimney with spit. Sometimes extra grown-ups pitch in to help feed them.
chimney-swift.social: Very social: in late summer they roost by the hundreds in one big chimney, swirling in at dusk.

spring.title: Back from South America
spring.body: Swifts return and pair up, gluing twig nests to chimney walls with their own spit.

summer.title: Chimney babies
summer.body: Chicks cling to the chimney wall and the parents zip in and out with balls of bugs.

fall.title: The big roost
fall.body: Families gather by the hundreds and pour into one chimney at dusk, like smoke in reverse, before flying south.

winter.title: Far, far away
winter.body: They're spending winter in the Amazon basin, thousands of miles south.

moths.young: No parenting at all: Mom lays her eggs on the right plant and the caterpillars take it from there.
moths.social: Solo. Grown-ups find each other by scent, sometimes from far away.

spring.title: Waking up
spring.body: Caterpillars and cocoons that waited out the winter are getting going again.

summer.title: Moth nights
summer.body: Warm nights are moth season. Females send out scents, and males follow them with their feathery antennae.

fall.title: Last flights
fall.body: The last moths of the year lay eggs that will wait out the winter.

winter.title: Waiting it out
winter.body: Most moths spend winter as eggs, caterpillars or cocoons, tucked in bark and leaf litter.

canada-goose.young: Both parents guard the goslings fiercely. The family stays together for their whole first year, and even migrates together.
canada-goose.social: Couples usually stay together for life. Families group up in bigger flocks, and goslings sometimes join big "day cares" watched by a few adults.

spring.title: On guard
spring.body: Mom sits on the nest while Dad stands guard nearby. Hissing is his whole job right now.

summer.title: Gosling parade
summer.body: Fuzzy goslings walk in a line between their parents, sometimes in big groups watched by a few grown-ups.

fall.title: Family flights
fall.body: This year's young fly with their parents now. Families stick together inside the big flocks.

winter.title: Still a family
winter.body: Families stay together all winter and split up next spring, when the parents nest again.

mallard.young: Mom raises the ducklings alone; the drakes leave once she's sitting on the eggs. Ducklings swim and find their own food within hours of hatching.
mallard.social: Couples form in fall and winter, then split up after nesting. Off-season, they're easygoing flock birds.

spring.title: Mom's on the nest
spring.body: Females are sitting on eggs, hidden in tall grass. The bright green-headed males hang out together without them.

summer.title: Duckling school
summer.body: Ducklings paddle after their mom in a row, learning where the good snacks are.

fall.title: Dating season
fall.body: Males are back in their bright colors and showing off to the females. Couples start forming now.

winter.title: Pairs on the pond
winter.body: Mallards swim around in pairs within the flock, ready to nest when spring comes.

brant.young: Brant nest in the Arctic tundra. Both parents tend the goslings, and families fly south together.
brant.social: Families stick together inside big winter flocks on the bays.

spring.title: Heading to the Arctic
spring.body: Brant fill up on sea lettuce before their long flight to nest in the Arctic.

summer.title: Tundra families
summer.body: They're raising goslings on the Arctic tundra, near the top of the world.

fall.title: Families arrive
fall.body: Brant families fly into the harbor together, parents and young side by side.

winter.title: Family groups
winter.body: In the big flocks on the bays, each family stays close together all winter.

double-crested-cormorant.young: Both parents raise the chicks in colonies on harbor islands. Chicks reach into a parent's throat to get their food.
double-crested-cormorant.social: Colony birds: they nest together, fish together and dry their wings side by side on posts.

spring.title: Island colonies
spring.body: Cormorants are building stick nests together on the harbor's islands.

summer.title: Chicks in the colony
summer.body: Chicks reach right into their parents' throats for fish. It's messy, but it works.

fall.title: Flying south
fall.body: Long lines of cormorants fly south along the coast, families and all.

winter.title: A few stay
winter.body: Most head south, but a few stick around and fish the harbor together.

ring-billed-gull.young: Both parents raise the chicks in big colonies. Many of the gulls you see here in summer are young ones not ready to nest yet.
ring-billed-gull.social: Colony birds and flock birds: always in a group.

spring.title: Off to the colonies
spring.body: Grown-ups head to nesting colonies inland and up north, often back to the same spot.

summer.title: The young ones stay
summer.body: Most ring-bills here in summer are teenagers, too young to nest, just hanging out.

fall.title: Everyone's back
fall.body: Grown-ups and this year's speckled young arrive in big flocks.

winter.title: Parking-lot crowds
winter.body: Ring-billed gulls gather by the hundreds on fields, beaches and parking lots.

common-tern.young: Both parents raise the chicks in noisy beach colonies. During courtship, the male brings the female a fish as a gift.
common-tern.social: Colony birds: they nest close together and all swoop together at anything that gets too close.

spring.title: Fish as gifts
spring.body: Males parade around the colony holding a little fish to impress a female.

summer.title: Beach babies
summer.body: Fluffy chicks hide in the sand while their parents dive for fish all day.

fall.title: Heading south
fall.body: Families leave together for South America. The young keep learning to fish along the way.

winter.title: Southern summer
winter.body: They're spending our winter on the coasts of South America.

great-blue-heron.young: Both parents raise the chicks in colonies of big stick nests high in the trees. The young leave the nest at around two months.
great-blue-heron.social: They nest together but hunt alone, each heron guarding their own stretch of shore.

spring.title: The heronry
spring.body: Herons are nesting together in treetop colonies on quiet islands.

summer.title: Tall chicks
summer.body: Gangly chicks wait in the nest, loudly greeting each parent who comes back with fish.

fall.title: Solo fishing
fall.body: The young are on their own, each heron standing alone at the water's edge.

winter.title: Hardy loners
winter.body: Some herons stay all winter, hunting alone in any water that isn't frozen.

black-crowned-night-heron.young: Both parents raise the chicks in colonies in the trees of the harbor islands. Chicks leave the nest in about six weeks.
black-crowned-night-heron.social: Social sleepers: they roost together in trees by day and go out to fish at dusk.

spring.title: Island colonies
spring.body: Night herons are nesting together in the trees of the harbor's little islands.

summer.title: Speckled young
summer.body: The young are brown and speckled, and look nothing like their parents yet.

fall.title: Sleepy groups
fall.body: Groups doze together in the trees by day and head out to fish at dusk.

winter.title: A few stay
winter.body: Most go south, but a few hunch together in the trees by the water all winter.

bufflehead.young: Buffleheads nest up north in old woodpecker holes. The ducklings jump out of the tree hole a day or two after hatching.
bufflehead.social: In winter they swim in small groups, diving at the same time like a little team.

spring.title: Off to the north
spring.body: Pairs fly north to nest in old woodpecker holes in northern forests.

summer.title: The big jump
summer.body: Up north, day-old ducklings leap out of their tree holes to follow their mom to water.

fall.title: Back in the harbor
fall.body: Small groups arrive and start diving together in the bays.

winter.title: Diving teams
winter.body: Little groups dive in near-unison and pop back up together.

mute-swan.young: Both parents raise the cygnets, who often ride on their parents' backs. The young usually stay with their parents through their first winter.
mute-swan.social: Couples usually stay together for years and defend their patch of water fiercely.

spring.title: The big nest
spring.body: Swan couples are building huge nests at the water's edge. The male guards it, wings raised.

summer.title: Back rides
summer.body: Fuzzy gray cygnets ride on their parents' backs and paddle close behind them.

fall.title: Gray teenagers
fall.body: The cygnets are almost full-size but still grayish brown, swimming with their parents.

winter.title: Family on the water
winter.body: Families often stay together all winter. In spring the parents send the young off to make their own way.

red-winged-blackbird.young: Females build nests in the cattails and do most of the work. A male may have several mates nesting in the territory he defends.
red-winged-blackbird.social: Bold singers in spring, then flock birds the rest of the year, often with grackles and starlings.

spring.title: The boss of the marsh
spring.body: Males sing from the cattails and flash their red patches to defend their territory.

summer.title: Cattail nests
summer.body: Females are raising chicks in nests woven between the reeds, while the males keep watch.

fall.title: Joining the flocks
fall.body: Families join big mixed flocks with grackles and starlings.

winter.title: Mostly south
winter.body: Most head south in giant flocks, but a few stay in the marshes.

white-tailed-deer.young: Fawns are born in late spring. Mom hides her spotted fawn in tall grass and comes back to nurse it. Fawns stay with their mom about a year, and daughters often stay longer.
white-tailed-deer.social: Moms, daughters and fawns live in family groups. Bucks hang out in bachelor groups in summer and go solo in the fall.

spring.title: Hidden fawns
spring.body: Fawns are being born. Mom hides each one in tall grass, where its spots help it stay still and unseen.

summer.title: Spotted kids
summer.body: Fawns follow their moms now. The bucks hang out together in bachelor groups, growing new antlers.

fall.title: Losing the spots
fall.body: Fawns trade their spots for a winter coat. The bucks split up and start sparring over the does.

winter.title: Family herds
winter.body: Moms, daughters and fawns stay together in small herds, sharing trails through the snow.

northern-mockingbird.young: Both parents raise the chicks. Dad often looks after the fledglings while Mom starts the next nest.
northern-mockingbird.social: They fiercely defend their territory all year, sometimes as a couple, sometimes on their own.

spring.title: Singing all night
spring.body: Single males sing their whole songbook, sometimes all night, to find a mate.

summer.title: Dad's turn
summer.body: Dad looks after the fledglings while Mom builds the next nest.

fall.title: Guarding the berries
fall.body: Each mockingbird claims a berry bush for the winter and chases everyone else away.

winter.title: Holding their ground
winter.body: Mockingbirds stay on their territory all winter, defending their berries.

northern-cardinal.young: Mom builds the nest and both parents feed the chicks. Dad often keeps feeding the fledglings while Mom starts another nest.
northern-cardinal.social: Couples often stay together all year. When courting, the male feeds the female seeds, beak to beak.

spring.title: Beak to beak
spring.body: Males are feeding their mates seeds beak to beak. It's how cardinals say "we're a team."

summer.title: Brown kids
summer.body: Young cardinals are brownish with dark beaks, following their red dad around and begging.

fall.title: Settling in
fall.body: The young find their own place, and couples settle in for the winter together.

winter.title: Winter flocks
winter.body: Cardinals sometimes gather in small flocks, bright red against the snow, couples still sticking close.

common-grackle.young: They nest in colonies in evergreens. Mom builds and sits on the nest; both parents feed the chicks.
common-grackle.social: Very social: they nest in groups and sleep in huge winter roosts.

spring.title: Puffed and squeaky
spring.body: Males puff up their glossy feathers and squeak like a rusty gate to impress the females.

summer.title: Family groups
summer.body: Fledglings follow their parents across the lawns, begging loudly.

fall.title: Giant flocks
fall.body: Grackles join huge mixed flocks with blackbirds and starlings.

winter.title: Mostly south
winter.body: Most head south in big flocks, but a few hang on through the winter.

gray-catbird.young: Both parents raise the chicks in a nest hidden deep in a thicket.
gray-catbird.social: Couples keep to their thicket and talk to each other in mews and long rambling songs.

spring.title: Back in the bushes
spring.body: Catbirds return and pair up, filling the thickets with long, rambling songs.

summer.title: Hidden nests
summer.body: They're raising chicks deep inside tangles and thickets.

fall.title: Berry fuel
fall.body: Catbirds fill up on berries before flying south.

winter.title: Down south
winter.body: Most spend winter in the southern U.S. and Central America.

song-sparrow.young: Both parents raise the chicks, often two or three broods a year.
song-sparrow.social: Neighbors learn each other's songs, and they answer a rival with a song both of them know.

spring.title: Song battles
spring.body: Neighboring males sing back and forth, matching each other's songs.

summer.title: Busy parents
summer.body: Parents raise brood after brood in nests low in the bushes.

fall.title: The young move out
fall.body: Young sparrows look for territories of their own, and some fly south for the winter.

winter.title: Hanging on
winter.body: Plenty stay all winter in brushy park edges, sometimes in loose groups.

american-kestrel.young: Both parents raise the chicks in a hole: a tree cavity, a nest box or a nook in a building. After leaving, the young hunt together near their parents for a while.
american-kestrel.social: Couples nest together, then mostly go solo for the winter.

spring.title: Nest holes
spring.body: Kestrel couples are moving into holes in trees, buildings and nest boxes.

summer.title: Hunting practice
summer.body: The fledglings hunt grasshoppers together near their parents.

fall.title: Heading out
fall.body: The young go off on their own, and many kestrels migrate south along the coast.

winter.title: Solo season
winter.body: Kestrels that stay spend the winter alone, each on their own hunting spot.

coopers-hawk.young: Both parents raise the chicks. The male brings almost all the food while the female, who's much bigger, guards the nest.
coopers-hawk.social: Couples nest together but hunt alone.

spring.title: Food delivery
spring.body: Males are bringing their mates food while the females build the nest and sit on the eggs.

summer.title: Loud youngsters
summer.body: The young leave the nest and screech for food from their parents.

fall.title: On their own
fall.body: This year's young are out hunting on their own, some migrating along the coast.

winter.title: Solo hunters
winter.body: Cooper's hawks spend winter alone, patrolling yards and parks.

peregrine-falcon.young: Both parents raise the chicks on a bare ledge high on a bridge or tower. The young practice flying and catching food from their parents in midair.
peregrine-falcon.social: Couples often stay together for life and keep their ledge for years.

spring.title: Ledge life
spring.body: Peregrine couples are sitting on eggs on bridges and skyscraper ledges.

summer.title: Midair handoffs
summer.body: Parents drop food to their young in midair to teach them to catch it.

fall.title: Leaving home
fall.body: The young head off on their own. Some travel a long way.

winter.title: Couples stay
winter.body: Most city pairs stay on their ledge all winter, together.

downy-woodpecker.young: Both parents carve the nest hole and feed the chicks. Dad often sits on the eggs at night.
downy-woodpecker.social: In winter they join little mixed flocks with titmice and nuthatches.

spring.title: Drumming
spring.body: Couples are drumming on branches and carving out a new nest hole together.

summer.title: Noisy holes
summer.body: Chicks chatter from inside the tree hole whenever a parent comes back with food.

fall.title: On their own
fall.body: The young go off alone, and each woodpecker carves a hole just for sleeping.

winter.title: Mixed flocks
winter.body: Downies travel with titmice and other little birds, all keeping an eye out together.

red-bellied-woodpecker.young: Both parents carve the nest hole and feed the chicks, who stay with them for a few weeks after leaving.
red-bellied-woodpecker.social: Couples share a territory and call to each other with rolling churrs.

spring.title: Tapping together
spring.body: The male drums and taps to show the female a good spot for a nest hole.

summer.title: Family weeks
summer.body: Fledglings follow their parents around for a few weeks, learning where the food is.

fall.title: Stashing food
fall.body: Each woodpecker hides nuts and seeds in bark cracks for later.

winter.title: Staying put
winter.body: Couples stay on their territory all winter, living on their stashes.

tufted-titmouse.young: Both parents raise the chicks, and sometimes last year's young stay to help with the new brood.
tufted-titmouse.social: Families stay together into winter and often lead little mixed flocks of other small birds.

spring.title: Fur for the nest
spring.body: Titmice line their nests with soft hair, sometimes plucked right off a sleeping raccoon or dog.

summer.title: Big family
summer.body: Families travel together, sometimes with a helper from last year.

fall.title: Flock leaders
fall.body: Families team up with chickadees and nuthatches, and the titmice often lead.

winter.title: Staying together
winter.body: Families stay together all winter, sounding the alarm when a hawk is near.

hermit-thrush.young: They nest on or near the ground in northern forests. Here, we meet them on migration and in winter.
hermit-thrush.social: Quiet loners: each thrush keeps to its own patch of forest floor.

spring.title: Passing through
spring.body: Thrushes stop in the parks on their way north to nest.

summer.title: Up north
summer.body: They're raising chicks in northern forests and singing their flute-like songs.

fall.title: Passing through again
fall.body: They stop by on the way south, each one quietly flipping leaves on its own.

winter.title: Winter loners
winter.body: A few stay all winter, each guarding its own berry tree.

yellow-rumped-warbler.young: They nest up north in evergreen forests. We meet them on migration and in winter.
yellow-rumped-warbler.social: Flock birds outside nesting season, often feeding in big groups.

spring.title: Passing through
spring.body: Warblers in fresh yellow-patched feathers pass through on their way north.

summer.title: Up north
summer.body: They're raising chicks in evergreen forests far north of the city.

fall.title: Big flocks
fall.body: Flocks pour through the parks, eating bugs and berries together.

winter.title: Berry flocks
winter.body: Some stay all winter in small flocks, living on waxy bayberries.

common-eastern-bumble-bee.young: A queen starts her colony alone in spring. Her first daughters grow up to be workers who raise the rest.
common-eastern-bumble-bee.social: A family of sisters that lasts just one summer. Only the new queens survive the winter, alone.

spring.title: Queen on her own
spring.body: Big queen bumble bees fly low, looking for a hole to start a new colony all by herself.

summer.title: Sister workers
summer.body: The queen's daughters do all the flower runs while she stays home and lays eggs.

fall.title: New queens
fall.body: The colony raises new queens. The old colony fades away as the weather cools.

winter.title: Solo sleepers
winter.body: Only the new queens survive, sleeping alone underground until spring.

western-honey-bee.young: One queen lays all the eggs. Her worker daughters feed the babies and run the hive.
western-honey-bee.social: Tens of thousands of sisters working together. They share news with a waggle dance.

spring.title: Swarm time
spring.body: Crowded hives split in two: the old queen leaves with half the bees to find a new home.

summer.title: Honey season
summer.body: The workers are making and storing honey for winter as fast as they can.

fall.title: Drones out
fall.body: The workers push the male bees out of the hive. There's not enough honey to go around.

winter.title: The cluster
winter.body: The bees huddle in a ball around their queen, shivering their muscles to keep warm.

eastern-carpenter-bee.young: Mom drills tunnels in wood and leaves pollen in each little room for her babies. She often stays near the nest as they grow.
eastern-carpenter-bee.social: Mostly solo, but some moms share their nest, and the young may spend winter in the tunnels together.

spring.title: Drilling
spring.body: Females are drilling perfectly round holes in wood. The males hover nearby, all buzz and no sting.

summer.title: Baby rooms
summer.body: Inside each tunnel, the babies grow in rooms stocked with pollen.

fall.title: Family tunnel
fall.body: The new adults stay close to the tunnel where they grew up.

winter.title: Snug in the wood
winter.body: They spend winter tucked inside the wood, sometimes several in one tunnel.

common-eastern-firefly.young: No parenting: firefly larvae hatch in the soil and spend a year or two growing up on their own.
common-eastern-firefly.social: Grown-ups talk in flashes: the male flashes a pattern, and the female answers from the grass.

spring.title: Underground
spring.body: Firefly larvae are finishing growing up in the soil. Some of them glow, too.

summer.title: Flash dating
summer.body: Males fly and flash their pattern; females answer from the grass. That's a firefly date.

fall.title: Larvae again
fall.body: This summer's eggs have hatched into larvae, hunting slugs in the soil.

winter.title: Waiting below
winter.body: Larvae wait out the winter underground.

blue-dasher.young: No parenting: Mom lays eggs in the water and the nymphs grow up underwater on their own.
blue-dasher.social: Males guard a sunny perch by the water and chase away other males.

spring.title: Underwater
spring.body: Nymphs are growing underwater in ponds, hunting tiny creatures.

summer.title: Perch guards
summer.body: Males guard their favorite perch by the pond, darting out to chase rivals away.

fall.title: Last flyers
fall.body: The last blue dashers of the year are out on warm days.

winter.title: Waiting in the pond
winter.body: Nymphs spend winter underwater, growing slowly until next summer.

large-milkweed-bug.young: No parenting: eggs hatch on milkweed and the bright young bugs feed together on the seed pods.
large-milkweed-bug.social: They gather in groups, often on the same milkweed pod.

spring.title: Back north
spring.body: The first milkweed bugs arrive from the south as the milkweed grows.

summer.title: Pod parties
summer.body: Groups of orange-and-black young and grown-ups cluster together on the milkweed pods.

fall.title: Crowded pods
fall.body: Groups crowd the open pods, and many fly south as it gets cold.

winter.title: Gone south
winter.body: Most head south for the winter. Few, if any, survive the cold here.

pond-slider.young: No parenting: Mom digs a nest on land and lays her eggs. The hatchlings dig their way out and head for water on their own.
pond-slider.social: Easygoing baskers: they pile up on logs together, sometimes stacked on each other's shells.

spring.title: Basking piles
spring.body: Turtles pile onto sunny logs together to warm up after winter.

summer.title: Nest digging
summer.body: Moms climb out of the pond to dig nests in soft ground, then head back to the water.

fall.title: Hatchlings
fall.body: Tiny hatchlings dig out and head for the water, all on their own.

winter.title: Pond-bottom nap
winter.body: They spend winter resting on the pond bottom, barely moving.

groundhog.young: Mom raises the pups alone in a burrow. They come out in late spring and move into burrows of their own by late summer.
groundhog.social: Solo, but neighbors often share the same big burrow systems over the years.

spring.title: Pups in the burrow
spring.body: Moms are raising pups underground. Dad isn't involved.

summer.title: Moving out
summer.body: Pups pop out and munch clover near the burrow, then dig homes of their own.

fall.title: Eating for winter
fall.body: Every groundhog is eating as much as possible before hibernating alone.

winter.title: Hibernating
winter.body: Groundhogs hibernate alone in their burrows, their hearts beating only a few times a minute.

orb-weavers.young: Mom wraps her eggs in a silk sac in the fall. The spiderlings hatch in spring and drift away on silk threads.
orb-weavers.social: Solo: each spider spins and guards her own web.

spring.title: Spiderling balloons
spring.body: Tiny spiderlings hatch and float away on silk threads to find their own spots.

summer.title: Growing webs
summer.body: Each spider builds a bigger web as she grows, often rebuilding it every night.

fall.title: Egg sacs
fall.body: Big grown-up spiders wrap their eggs in silk sacs before winter.

winter.title: Waiting in the sac
winter.body: The eggs wait out the winter in their silk sacs, tucked in safe spots.
